name: Vectorscan
baseline: Snort 3 built without Vectorscan (Snort's built-in fallback pattern matcher; the commit message does not name the fallback algorithm)
workload: End-to-end network throughput of Snort 3.1.84.0 running on OpenWrt routers with a roughly 22 MB community ruleset, measured with and without the Vectorscan 5.4.11 package (download speed through the router in IDS and IPS mode, n=3).
claimed_speedup: GL.iNet GL-MT6000 (MediaTek, flogic): IDS mode 91.2 Mbit/s without vs 331.0 Mbit/s with Vectorscan (3.6x), IPS mode 30.0 vs 52.9 Mbit/s (1.8x). Raspberry Pi 5B (bcm2712): IPS mode 164.3 vs 232.8 Mbit/s (1.4x).
hardware: GL.iNet GL-MT6000 router SoC (flogic/glinet_gl-mt6000, kernel 6.6.26) and Raspberry Pi 5B (bcm2712, kernel 6.1.86); exact CPU model strings not given
stars_or_usage: 766 stars; packaged in OpenWrt, used with Snort 3
tradeoffs: Multi-pattern (set) matching library with a libpcre-like syntax subset: no backreferences or arbitrary lookaround, and it reports match end offsets, so it is not a drop-in replacement for a backtracking engine such as std::regex or PCRE. It exists mainly to bring Hyperscan to non-x86 CPUs (ARM NEON/ASIMD, ARM SVE2, Power VSX, plus a SIMDe backend); on x86 it keeps the upstream Hyperscan code paths. Large compiled databases and long compile times are the usual cost of the hybrid-automata approach. Fork of Intel Hyperscan; per the project README, Hyperscan versions after 5.4 are going closed-source, so Vectorscan is the open-source line (the README says its ARM port was rejected upstream).
caveats: The only numeric comparison reachable is a packager's commit message in the OpenWrt packages repository (third party, not the project's own repo). It measures Snort 3 as a whole through a router with a speedtest script, not the regex engine in isolation, and the baseline is 'Snort without Vectorscan' with the fallback matcher unnamed, so the speedups are not regex-engine speedups. Compiler, flags and exact CPU models are not stated, no benchmark code is public, n=3 per cell, and the numbers are ARM-router numbers where Hyperscan itself cannot run. No comparison against std::regex, RE2, PCRE or Hyperscan was found: the project wiki has a Benchmarks page but its body did not load here and the Arm blog post 'Accelerating deep packet inspection with NEON on Arm Neoverse' was blocked by the egress policy (snippet only, no numbers seen). benchmarks/benchmarks.cpp in the repo is an internal microbenchmark of its own primitives, not a baseline comparison. The patch's author date reads May 2023 while the commit message cites Snort 3.1.84.0 and Vectorscan 5.4.11, so the date and version details were not reconciled.

name: Vince's CSV Parser
baseline: fast-cpp-csv-parser (also rapidcsv and Glaze's CSV reader in the same suite)
workload: Google Benchmark median real time on a generated 8-column CSV (id,city,state,category,amount,quantity,flag,note) of 500K and 5M rows in clean, quoted and multiline profiles: raw row count/read, one-pass row materialization, materialize plus multi-pass aggregation, and DataFrame load and load+edit+save against rapidcsv.
claimed_speedup: Materialization (single parser worker), 5M clean: 739.6 ms vs 2,105 ms for fast-cpp-csv-parser (2.8x, derived from page data); 5M quoted 930.6 ms vs 2,489 ms. Materialize+aggregation 5M clean 1,251 ms vs 2,252 ms, 5M quoted 1,517 ms vs 3,090 ms. Positional read with 4 parser workers overtakes fast-cpp-csv-parser (5M clean 702.2 ms vs 915.1 ms; spec-8 605.0 ms). Versus rapidcsv: DataFrame load 1.56x (500K clean) to 4.53x (5M multiline) faster, load+save 2.17x to 3.58x faster. Versus Glaze CSV reader: 5M clean materialization 739.6 ms vs 1,972 ms. It loses on small raw reads: 500K clean count 146.5 ms vs 81.8 ms and read 164.9 ms vs 82.8 ms for fast-cpp-csv-parser.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.50 (Visual Studio 2026), Windows SDK 10.0.26100.0, C++20, AVX2 enabled, CMake Release build, CSV_ENABLE_THREADS=ON, Google Benchmark 1.8.5; Glaze targets built as C++23
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i5-12400 (12 logical CPUs, about 2.5 GHz), Windows 11 Home 25H2, Samsung 990 EVO SSD
tradeoffs: Fully RFC 4180-compliant out of the box (embedded newlines, quoted fields), which fast-cpp-csv-parser does not support and which costs raw throughput. Dynamic row model with string-valued fields and optional type conversion rather than compile-time typed columns. Fast paths use memory-mapped files and a speculative parallel parser (after Ge et al., SIGMOD 2019) with a background thread, 10 MB default chunks, so it uses more cores and more memory than a single-threaded streaming reader. C++11 minimum, C++20 recommended; ships a DataFrame and a CSV writer.
caveats: Project's own benchmarks, run on one machine, one OS and one compiler (Windows/MSVC), so ordering may shift on GCC or Clang and on Linux. The README itself says fast-cpp-csv-parser wins the smaller raw read and count tests (500K rows) and only overtakes with 4 or more parser workers or in materialization. The rapidcsv comparison pits csv-parser's filename path (memory-mapped, background-threaded reader) against rapidcsv's single-threaded Document, so background and parallel threads are part of the speedup (all tables use median real time, not CPU time). No comparison against std::getline or any libstdc++/libc++ code was found, so the suggested std::getline baseline is not covered. Higher-level claim 'likely one of the fastest general-purpose C++ CSV ETL libraries' is the author's wording. Benchmark inputs are generated, not real-world data (the separate Kaggle-file timings, such as 1.4 GB in 0.48 s, have no baseline). Compiler and CPU are stated; exact optimization flags beyond Release and AVX2 come from the CMake defaults, not a printed flag line.
